questions.question: In a steady climb at flight-path angle γ (with thrust aligned along the flight path), what are the force balance equations along and perpendicular to the flight path?
options: T = D + mg sin γ and L = mg cos γ
T = D + mg cos γ and L = mg sin γ
T = D and L = mg + T sin γ
T = D − mg sin γ and L = mg cos γ
questions.explanation: Weight acts straight down, so resolving it along the inclined flight path puts a backward component mg sin γ opposing thrust and a perpendicular component mg cos γ opposing lift. Swapping sine and cosine fails the level-flight check at γ = 0; subtracting mg sin γ describes a descent rather than a climb.

questions.section: Excess power, steepest climb, and fastest climb
questions.question: An aircraft weighing mg = 50,000 N flies at V = 80 m/s with power available PA = 900 kW and power required PR = 500 kW. What are its rate of climb and flight-path angle?
questions.explanation: Excess power is PA − PR = 400 kW = 400,000 W, so R/C = 400,000/50,000 = 8.0 m/s and sin γ = 8.0/80 = 0.10, giving γ = 5.74°. 18.0 m/s divides PA alone by weight; 0.10° confuses radians with degrees; 5.0 m/s divides excess power in kW (400) by V (80) instead of dividing excess power in W by weight mg.

questions.section: Excess power, steepest climb, and fastest climb
questions.question: A twin-engine aircraft loses one of its two identical engines while climbing at a fixed airspeed. Why does its rate of climb drop by much more than 50 percent?
options: PA drops by half while PR stays unchanged, so excess power PA − PR shrinks by more than half
Drag doubles automatically whenever one engine shuts down
Aircraft weight doubles per operating engine, which halves PR
Propulsive efficiency falls to zero on the remaining engine
questions.explanation: Because R/C = (PA − PR)/(mg), cutting PA in half leaves the full drag power PR to subtract from the smaller available power. For instance, if PA = 100 and PR = 40, excess power drops from 60 to 10 (an 83 percent loss).

questions.section: Excess power, steepest climb, and fastest climb
questions.question: For a jet aircraft with constant thrust available TA, at what airspeed does the steepest climb angle γmax occur, and how does it compare with the best-rate-of-climb speed?
options: At VTR,min, which is slower than the best-rate-of-climb speed
At VPR,min, which is faster than the best-rate-of-climb speed
At the exact same speed as the best-rate-of-climb speed
At the maximum level-flight speed Vmax
questions.explanation: With flat TA, sin γ = (TA − TR)/(mg) is largest where TR is smallest, at VTR,min. Because R/C = V sin γ multiplies excess thrust by V, the peak climb rate shifts to a higher speed. At Vmax, excess thrust and climb angle are zero.

questions.section: Obstacle clearance with one engine out
questions.question: A twin-jet weighing 100,000 N has CD,0 = 0.020 and K = 0.045. With one engine out at sea level, its remaining thrust is TA = 10,000 N. What is its steepest climb angle γmax?
questions.explanation: Using sin γmax = TA/(mg) − 2√(K CD,0) gives 10,000/100,000 − 2√(0.045 × 0.020) = 0.100 − 0.060 = 0.040, so γmax = arcsin(0.040) = 2.29°. 5.74° leaves out drag completely; 3.44° uses 0.060 alone; 9.21° adds the two terms instead of subtracting.

questions.section: Obstacle clearance with one engine out
questions.question: An aircraft climbs after liftoff at its steepest one-engine-out angle of 2.29° (tan 2.29° = 0.0400). An 80 m radio tower stands 1,800 m beyond the liftoff point. Does the aircraft clear the tower?
options: No, it gains only 72.0 m over 1,800 m and falls 8.0 m short
Yes, it gains 90.0 m and clears the tower by 10.0 m
Yes, because any positive climb angle clears an obstacle ahead
No, because 2.29° is too shallow for steady flight
questions.explanation: Height gained over 1,800 m is Δh = 1,800 × tan(2.29°) = 1,800 × 0.0400 = 72.0 m, which is below the 80 m tower height (required angle is arctan(80/1,800) = 2.54°). A positive climb angle guarantees climbing, not clearing a specific obstacle.

questions.question: How are the absolute ceiling and the service ceiling defined?
options: Absolute ceiling is where (R/C)max = 0; service ceiling is where (R/C)max = 0.5 m/s (100 ft/min)
Service ceiling is where (R/C)max = 0; absolute ceiling is where (R/C)max = 0.5 m/s
Absolute ceiling is where Vmax reaches Mach 1; service ceiling is the tropopause
Both ceilings occur where TA = 0
questions.explanation: At the absolute ceiling, excess power vanishes and (R/C)max = 0 (reachable only in infinite time). The service ceiling sits slightly lower, at the practical limit where (R/C)max = 0.5 m/s (100 ft/min). At both ceilings TA is still positive, matching TR,min at the absolute ceiling and exceeding it at the service ceiling.

questions.question: A jet has sea-level total thrust n T0 = 40,000 N, minimum thrust required TR,min = 10,000 N, and lapse exponent mad = 1.0. What is the density ratio ρc/ρ0 at its absolute ceiling?
questions.explanation: At the jet absolute ceiling, TA = TR,min, so n T0 (ρc/ρ0)mad = TR,min. With mad = 1.0, ρc/ρ0 = 10,000/40,000 = 0.25. 0.50 takes a square root; 0.75 subtracts from 1; 0.125 divides by 2.
